## Score Descriptions:

### Vulnerability:

```{r}
#| echo: false
# Define the path to the potential image
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), ".pdf", ".png")
img_path <- here::here(paste0("figures/White hake/total_vulnerability_map_all", ext))

# Store the TRUE/FALSE result 
has_figure <- file.exists(img_path)
```

```{r,echo=FALSE, fig.align='center'}
#| lightbox: true
#| eval: !expr has_figure
#| fig-cap: "Vulnerability on the Northeast Shelf for White hake"
#| label: fig-vuln
#| out-width: "85%"
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-pos: "H"
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), ".pdf", ".png")
knitr::include_graphics(here::here(paste0("figures/White hake/total_vulnerability_map_all", ext)))
```

Mean Vulnerability for white hake was **Moderate** (4.02 +/- 1.98) (@fig-sum-tab). Vulnerability was High over Georges Bank and Moderate along the coasts of the Gulf of Maine (@fig-vuln). Vulnerability scores did not change when exposure was calculated using only factors important to the species distribution (@fig-sum-tab).

In the previous Assessment, white hake also received a Moderate score [@hare2016vulnerability].

### Climate Exposure:


```{r,echo=FALSE, fig.align='center'}
#| lightbox: true
#| eval: !expr has_figure
#| fig-cap: "Exposure on the Northeast Shelf for White hake"
#| label: fig-exp
#| out-width: "85%"
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-pos: "H"
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), ".pdf", ".png")
knitr::include_graphics(here::here(paste0("figures/White hake/total_exposure_map_all", ext)))
```

Mean exposure for White hake was **Moderate** (2.01 +/- 0.99) (@fig-sum-tab). Exposure was Very High over Georges Bank and Moderate along the coast of Georges Bank. Farther from the coast, scores were Low (@fig-exp). These patterns were driven by bottom temperature, salinity, and oxygen exposure (@fig-fact-exp). 

In the previous Assessment, White hake received a High exposure score. This previous score was driven by high sea surface temperature and ocean acidification exposure [@hare2016vulnerability].

```{r}

# Define the path to the potential image
```

```{r,echo=FALSE, fig.align='center'}
#| lightbox: true
#| eval: !expr has_figure
#| fig-cap: "Exposure and Monthly Variability Based on Factors critical to White hake distributions"
#| label: fig-exp-imp
#| out-width: "85%"
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-pos: "H"

knitr::include_graphics(here::here(paste0("figures/White hake/total_exposure_map_timeseries_imp", ext)))
```

Bottom temperature, oxygen, and salinity as well as small and large zooplankton biomass were important dynamic drivers of white hake distribution (@fig-sum-tab). White hake are a demersal groundfish species. Their inshore and offshore movements are dictated by temperature and prey movements [@langton1994selected]. Adults are generalist piscivores [@langton1994selected] [@nozeres2015review]. When only these factors were used to calculate exposure, scores remained Moderate (1.89 +/- 0.99) (@fig-sum-tab, @fig-exp-imp).

### Biological Sensitivity:

```{r}
#| echo: false
# Define the path to the potential image
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), ".pdf", ".png")
img_path <- here::here(paste0("figures/White hake/sensitivity_map", ext))

# Store the TRUE/FALSE result 
has_figure <- file.exists(img_path)
```

```{r,echo=FALSE, fig.align='center'}
#| lightbox: true
#| eval: !expr has_figure
#| fig-cap: "Sensitivity on the Northeast Shelf"
#| label: fig-sens
#| out-width: "85%"
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-pos: "H"
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), ".pdf", ".png")
knitr::include_graphics(here::here(paste0("figures/White hake/sensitivity_map", ext)))
```

White hake received a **Moderate** sensitivity score, with a certainty of 59%. Four attributes had scores greater than 2.5: Stock Size (3), Juvenile Habitat Requirements (2.9), Population Growth Rate (2.8), and Spawning Cycle (2.8) (@fig-sum-tab).

Spawning occurs in the spring months along the continental shelf near Georges Bank and the Mid Atlantic Bight [@fahay1989white]. Juveniles transition from pelagic to demersal at approximately two months, where eelgrass becomes an important habitat. These habitats are highly vulnerable [@guyant2022northeast]. White hake reach maturity at 2.5-2.8 year and have lifespans of approximately 20 years [@nefsc2013saw56]. The stock is under a rebuilding plan, but is not overfished nor is overfishing occurring [@nefsc2025whitehake].

White hake also received a Moderate sensitivity score in the 2016 Climate Vulnerability Assessment. This was driven by Stock Status, Population Growth Rate, and Spawning Cycle, similar to our results.

### Directional Effect:

Experts predicted that white hake will be **negatively** impacted by climate change. Certainty was 70%. This is similar to the results of the previous Assessment [@hare2016vulnerability]. White hake have a narrow temperature preference (9-13 °C) and as a result, distributions have been shifting northward as bottom waters warm [@lafreniere2023what]. Recruitment is strongly linked to circulation patterns, which may be impacted by future change [@han2008dispersion] [@ings2008episodic].

## Climate Effects on Abundance and Distribution

White hake are a common groundfish species in the Gulf of Maine, which is warming faster than most of the world’s oceans [@pershing2021climate]. In response to warming in the Gulf of Maine, white hake show a preference for narrow temperature (9-13°C) and depth (55-100 m) ranges and display a gradual northward movement in their center of gravity [@lafreniere2023what]. @nye2009changing observed a range contraction in white hake in the Gulf of Maine. White hake may be affected by changes in circulation patterns. Small white hake larvae have been collected in early summer in a Gulf Stream warm core ring seaward of southern Scotian Shelf and southeast of Georges Bank. Patterns of strong recruitment have been linked to the strength of the Labrador Current on the Great Banks and strong onshore transport and downwelling conditions in coastal Newfoundland [@han2008dispersion] [@ings2008episodic].

## Life History Synopsis

White hake are a groundfish species inhabiting deep water from Newfoundland to the Mid-Atlantic Bight [@chang1999essential]. Males reach maturity at 2.5 years and females at 2.8 years; both males and females have a lifespan of around 20 years of age [@nefsc2013saw56]. In the Gulf of Maine, white hake of all ages tend to migrate inshore in warmer months and disperse into deeper waters in colder months, while hake in the south move offshore to spawn in the spring; fall movements may be linked to prey movements [@langton1994selected]. Based on the distribution and abundance of pelagic juveniles, as well as circulation patterns throughout the region, @fahay1989white suggested that the southern portion of the stock (below the Gulf of St. Lawrence) spawns in early spring (April-May) in deep waters along the continental slope, primarily off southern Georges Bank and the Mid-Atlantic Bight. White hake eggs are buoyant, and hatch in the water column in 3-7 days [@fahay1983guide]. Larvae may be affected by oceanographic conditions like warm core rings, the Gulf Stream, and Labrador Current for transport [@han2008dispersion] [@ings2008episodic]. White hake prefer temperatures between 7-20°C [@chang1999essential]. Eggs, larvae, and early juveniles are pelagic; older juveniles and adults are demersal. Most catches occur in Canadian waters at depths between 175 to 375 m with no differences between mature and immature hake. In the Gulf of Maine, depth preferences are 55-100 m [@fahay1989white] [@nozeres2015review]. Juvenile white hake settle to the bottom at around 2 months of age. Pelagic juveniles are in the upper water column during the daytime. Demersal juveniles inhabit muddy and fine grained sandy bottom sediment [@chang1999essential] [@fahay1989white]. Demersal juveniles feed primarily on polychaetes, shrimps, and other crustaceans [@bowman1981food]. Adults feed on fish, including juveniles of their own and similar species (silver hake), Atlantic herring, Gulf Stream flounder, and possibly alewife, shrimps, krill, and other crustaceans [@langton1994selected] [@nozeres2015review]. The white hake fishery is managed as a single stock by the New England Fisheries Management Council, under the Northeast Multispecies (Small-Mesh) Fishery Management Plan. The stock is under a rebuilding plan, but is not overfished and overfishing is not occurring [@nefsc2025whitehake].
